doc.title: Arthur Davis and Andy Mosley Interview, 1960-01-12

title: How the hammer song was sung while laying steel
summary: Speakers explain the lead and background singing and that axes beating a log supplied the rhythm for laying track.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: That was his first appearance when he was in on the background. Nothing but my hammer boy. I'm a ring. Well, nothing but my hammer boy. I'm a ring.

Now, it's closer to that song that he's going to probably laugh at where I made him laugh at on the background because I heard it was a long song where I was singing. He made him laugh at what? He made him laugh at what? Because the song was long. He kept on singing. I'm a ring.

hammering. Well I wasn't too familiar with this song. I figured this other boy, Rose Gellie Charles, was more familiar with it. Riding the Mason, which we call Louisiana. They was participating in it and he sang it. He was the vocalist on this song.
What were y'all doing? Were you swinging hammers or axes?

Yeah, we were swinging axes and we were using a log as a decoder that most of it was tracking, laying steel. That's the reason they call it that where the hammer ran. Oh I see. In terms of the timer that what you're on the background you're hearing now that well the guy's is beating on a log with some axes that they're with.

Yeah. Now that was more of the sound, that's the sound song all the way through. And that was the first appearance as I foretold you that when Mr. Austin had made his tour on the phone there. Oh yeah. That was the first record. I don't remember a man sitting in on it.
